newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian forex market volumes poised for sharp rise.
newsitem.headline: Indian forex market volumes poised for sharp rise.

text.p: India's forex markets are poised to see a sharp growth in turnover but a dearth of market makers and illiquidity continue to skew the market, bankers said.
"The (forex) turnover has increased tremendously compared to 1991-92 levels," Moses Harding, vice president of the private IndusInd Bank in Bombay said on Tuesday.
"With increased risk management awareness among even medium-term corporates, volumes are climbing," he said. Daily volumes are currently between $1.0-1.5 billion, bankers said.

O.P. Sodhani, former executive director of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), told the annual meeting of the Forex Association of India at the weekend he expected volumes to spurt following recent RBI relaxations on access to external borrowings.
"A larger number of companies will now be exposed to foreign currency risks," Sodhani said.
Analysts said Indian firms with good ratings now preferred cheaper external debt to costlier rupee funds.
RBI officials said the entry of new banks both Indian and foreign with international exposure has brought expertise and sophistication in the market.
"The level of awareness and expertise among the clientele and banks has taken a quantum jump," an RBI official said.
But the officials said it was regrettable that there were only a handful of market makers, most of them foreign, despite a sharp rise in activity in recent years.

"There seems to be no reason why banks with the bulk having a merchant base should not develop as market makers, thereby giving the markets more depth and width and in the process giving customers a better deal," an RBI official said.

P.K. Pain, general manager of the State Bank of India, India's largest commercial bank, said many state-run banks, which dominate the merchant business, were reluctant to invest in foreign exchange infrastructure as they were not sure about the profitability of this operation.
He suggested these banks should integrate profit-making money market operations with foreign exchange dealing.
"Depth, discipline and more market makers - that's what we need," said S.V. Pinto, chief forex dealer at the state-run Canara Bank, one of the market makers and an active player.
RBI officials said some banks did not update their quotes continuously or deal at the rates they quoted on the screen.
India's foreign exchange market is very illiquid and one bank's dollar purchase often pulls down the rupee by a few paise, making market participants at large uneasy.

"Perhaps the market will continue to remain so (illiquid) as forward rates are determined by demand and supply forces," Sodhani said. The remedy would be to allow authorised foreign exchange dealers to borrow and lend overseas, he said.
